source.source_project: A — richer teaching interface with handwritten dynamics

preservation: Original lesson content is preserved verbatim as structured data. Issue metadata accompanies it; do not present the original wording as a reviewed course.

legacy_seeded_progress.note: Historical demo defaults; not evidence of user learning and must not be carried into a fresh learner profile.

known_issues.issue: Text says each simulation tick writes to a fresh mjData buffer. Typical stepping mutates the existing allocated data object; the next paragraph correctly emphasizes allocation-free reset.
Calling the compiled model immutable is too absolute. Treat it as shared configuration by convention; supported fields can be changed, with recomputation constraints.
Claim that sensors are evaluated at the end of the step oversimplifies stage-dependent sensor evaluation and the relation between derived quantities and integrated state.
The stated inspection point for mj_step1/mj_step2 needs verification against the actual pipeline and integrator limitations.
implicitfast is described as using a diagonal approximation. Verify the actual derivative approximation in official computation documentation before publication.
50 Hz means one action every 20 ms, not every 4 ms. 4 ms corresponds to 250 Hz.
actuator_force = gear * ctrl conflates scalar actuator force with generalized force after transmission. Explain the actuator force law and moment-arm mapping separately.
The description of a position actuator as a first-order servo is imprecise and should distinguish a force law from actuator activation dynamics.
The environment snippet omits observation_space, reset, _obs, _reward, termination logic, and a trainer. It is an outline, not runnable training code.
The numerical claim that nine out of ten dynamics bugs are axes or collision pairs has no supplied evidence; retain it only as a clearly labeled heuristic without the statistic.

modules.title: The MuJoCo mental model
modules.description: How a scene is compiled, stepped, and observed.

lessons.title: The MJCF mental model
lessons.summary: MJCF is a description, not a program. The compiler turns your XML into a reusable physics model.
takeaways: MJCF describes bodies, joints, geoms, and actuators as a tree.
The compiler resolves defaults and compiles reusable functions and constraints.
One XML file can contain multiple assets and keyframes, but exactly one <mujoco> root.
body: MuJoCo separates the model — what the robot is — from the data — where it is right now. Your MJCF file becomes an mjModel at load time, while every simulation tick writes into a fresh mjData buffer.
This split is the reason large-scale learning is fast: resetting an environment reallocates nothing. The compiled model is immutable and shared, while data is cheap to reset and copy.
Start every debugging session by asking which layer is wrong. A malformed pose is usually a data problem. A broken inertia, missing joint, or impossible contact is usually a model problem.
lessons.code:
<mujoco model="two_link_arm">
  <compiler angle="radian" autolimits="true"/>
  <option timestep="0.002" integrator="implicitfast"/>
  <worldbody>
    <body name="upper" pos="0 0 0.3">
      <joint name="shoulder" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>
      <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 1 0 0" size=".06" mass=".8"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>

lessons.title: Bodies, joints & geoms
lessons.summary: The body tree defines kinematics. Joints connect degrees of freedom. Geoms define collision.
takeaways: Every body has a pose relative to its parent; only joints add degrees of freedom.
A freejoint contributes 7 qpos and 6 qvel coordinates.
Geoms own collision geometry; they inherit inertia from mass and shape.
body: Bodies are frames. Without a joint, a child body is welded to its parent. Add a hinge and the relative transform becomes parameterised by one angle; add a slide and it becomes a translation.

Geoms are primitives: plane, sphere, capsule, box, cylinder, ellipsoid, mesh. Collision only happens between pairs that survive the contype/conaffinity filter. In newer MuJoCo versions, explicit <pair> elements give you finer control.
Sites are non-colliding frames that are perfect for sensors, targets, and end effectors. Keep sites tiny and visual; keep geoms physical.
lessons.code:
<body name="cart" pos="0 0 .18">
  <joint name="slide" type="slide" axis="1 0 0"
         range="-2 2" damping=".05"/>
  <geom name="chassis" type="box"
        size=".25 .15 .1" mass="1.2"/>
  <site name="cart_imu" pos="0 0 .12" size=".02"/>
  <body name="pole" pos="0 0 .11">
    <joint name="hinge" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>
    <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0 0 .9"
          size=".025" mass=".2"/>
  </body>
</body>

lessons.title: Reading qpos, qvel & ctrl
lessons.summary: Every simulation exposes three arrays. Learning their layouts prevents most shape bugs.
takeaways: qpos holds generalised positions; for a hinge this is an angle, for a freejoint a position + quaternion.
qvel holds degrees of freedom velocities — one fewer than the freejoint position count.
control is the actuator command vector; it is not the same as force.
body: For a serial arm with two hinges, nq equals nv equals two. For a floating box, nq grows to seven while nv is six. Never infer one count from the other unless every joint is hinge or slide.
Use model.jnt_qposadr and model.jnt_dofadr to write into the correct slots instead of hard-coding indices. This is the difference between a demo and an environment you can trust.

ctrl is a command, not a force. A motor turns ctrl into torque via gear and gains; a position actuator solves for the force that tracks a target. Inspect actuator_force when a robot behaves strangely.
lessons.code:
import mujoco as mj

model = mj.MjModel.from_xml_path("scene.xml")
data = mj.MjData(model)

print("nq / nv / nu:", model.nq, model.nv, model.nu)

def act(q_target):
    data.ctrl[:] = q_target
    mj.mj_step(model, data)
    return data.qpos.copy(), data.sensordata.copy()

modules.title: Dynamics & contact
modules.description: The solver pipeline, constraint models, and numerical health.

lessons.title: Inside a simulation step
lessons.summary: Forward kinematics, collision detection, constraint solving, integration. In that order.
takeaways: The pipeline is deterministic: kinematics → collision → constraints → forward dynamics → integration.
Warm-starting accelerates convergence and is why consecutive calls reuse previous contact forces.
Step cost grows with active constraints, not just the number of bodies.
body: mj_step first propagates the kinematic tree, then detects collisions, assembles constraint rows, solves for constraint forces, computes accelerations, and integrates. Sensors are evaluated at the end of the step.

Most surprises come from collision: a convex hull that is too large, a self-collision filter that should be disabled, or a pair not included in the broadphase. Turn on contact-point visualisation before touching solver settings.
When the solver fails to converge you get soft interpenetration or jitter. Use mj_step1 / mj_step2 when you need to inspect data between constraint assembly and integration.

lessons.title: Contacts, gaps & solref
lessons.summary: Make contact stable by understanding margin, gap, solimp and solref — in that order.
takeaways: margin begins to generate constraint rows before the actual contact; gap is deprecated in newer models.
solref encodes time constant and damping ratio, not stiffness like a game-engine spring.
Friction is a cone unless you switch to an elliptic cone; condim controls the number of friction rows.
body: MuJoCo allows small penetration as a solver-tolerant constraint. The margin value decides how early the constraint becomes active, smoothing the transition and improving convergence on dense contact.
solref = [timeconst, dampratio]. A larger time constant makes contact softer. For a heavy robot, refine the physical collision shapes before making the contact artificially compliant.
For grasping, friction and condim matter more than restitution. Use condim=4 for torsional friction and 6 for rolling friction. Test the same object at multiple masses before committing gains.
lessons.code:
<geom name="cube" type="box" size=".06 .06 .06"
      mass=".2" friction="1.2 .05 .01"
      condim="4" solref=".008 1" solimp=".9 .95 .003"/>

<contact>
  <pair geom1="wall" geom2="cube" friction=".2"/>
</contact>

lessons.title: Choosing a solver & integrator
lessons.summary: Newton, CG, PGS, Euler, RK4 and implicitfast: sensible defaults and when to deviate.
takeaways: Use Newton + implicitfast as a modern default for contact-rich robots.
Solve the constraint problem well before shrinking timestep to hide jitter.
Timestep is a control decision as much as a numerical one; document the control frequency.
body: Newton solves the full convex constraint problem using a Hessian. CG is cheaper for large, sparse scenes. PGS is the classic fallback and can respond differently on tricky friction pyramids.
implicitfast damps velocity-dependent forces with a diagonal approximation without the cost of full implicit integration. It is stable enough for most model-based control and reinforcement learning.
Sensor data is only as resolved as your timestep. If you intend to control at 50 Hz, act every 4 ms but step the physics at 0.5 ms and accumulate, rather than increasing frame_skip blindly.
lessons.code:
<option timestep=".001"
        integrator="implicitfast"
        solver="Newton"
        iterations="8"
        tolerance="1e-9"/>

<!-- Log the effective control rate -->
<custom>
  <numeric name="ctrl_hz" data="50"/>
</custom>

modules.title: Actuation & control
modules.description: Turn stable dynamics into competent, inspectable behaviour.

lessons.title: PD gains that don't explode
lessons.summary: Pick gains from natural frequency and damping ratio, then verify with a step response.
takeaways: kp = I·ω² and kd = 2·ζ·I·ω is a defensible starting point for a joint-space servo.
Clamp torque at the actuator, not at the controller, so the model reports what actually happened.
Gravity compensation is not optional for heavy arms.
body: A PD controller is a spring-damper on position error. Choose the damping ratio first: ζ ≈ 0.7–1.0 for a settling response without visible oscillation. Then select ω below the actuator bandwidth.
Gain scheduling is a legitimate tool. A nearly straight arm has different inertia than a folded one; if one gain set must cover both, run a frequency sweep across the workspace.
The oscillation you see may not be your gains. Check for a delay in the control loop, a too-large timestep, or a position actuator whose gain is far above its forcerange.

lessons.title: Actuator tuning
lessons.summary: Motor, position, velocity, general: understand what ctrl is actually commanding.
takeaways: Motor applies force proportional to control; gear scales the transmitted force.
Position actuators add their own internal servo with kp and kv; nested PD can fight itself.
Always set plausible ctrlrange and forcerange; unsupervised commands hide broken controllers.
body: An actuator is a transmission plus a force law. For a direct-drive motor, actuator_force = gear * ctrl. For position control, MuJoCo internally uses a first-order servo, exposed through kp and kv.
Do not stack a large hand-written PD on top of a position actuator. Pick one abstraction and measure the resulting actuator_force. If a number is pinned at the limit, the controller is saturated.
Torque limits belong in the model. This keeps training rollouts physically constrained and makes a learned policy transferable instead of relying on software clip values.

lessons.title: MuJoCo for reinforcement learning
lessons.summary: Wrap a compiled model into a deterministic, vectorisable environment.
takeaways: A reset must clear the data buffer; qpos0 is only a convenient initial keyframe.
Control frequency should be explicit in the environment contract.
Observation scaling and termination conditions are part of your reward design.
body: The clean pattern is: compile once, allocate data once, reset in place. Use model.qpos0 or a keyframe as the nominal pose, then add task-appropriate initial state noise.

Separate action normalisation from physical limits. Policies usually produce bounded, dimensionless actions; the environment is responsible for mapping them to ctrl ranges and choosing control frequency.
Log qpos, qvel, actuator_force, and contact counts alongside rewards. Most learning pathologies look obvious in those traces, long before a reward curve turns the corner.

lessons.title: Robustness & sim-to-real
lessons.summary: Randomise the model, not just the state. Validate on the edges of your distribution.
takeaways: Domain randomisation should target parameters with real uncertainty: mass, friction, delay, actuation.
Randomising everything makes learning slower and hides systematic model error.
Validate on nominal, edge, and adversarial conditions separately.
body: Start from a measured nominal model. Randomise mass within a defensible range, friction within its cone, and actuator strength from datasheet tolerance. Add observation delay only after checking the real control loop.
Use procedural reset noise for generalisation inside a task, and parameter noise for robustness to a different robot. They solve different problems and should be logged separately.
A policy that only works at the midpoint of its training distribution is not robust. Build a regression suite of seeds, terrain variants, and payloads that run on every checkpoint.

lessons.title: Debug like a roboticist
lessons.summary: A repeatable visual and numerical workflow for when the robot misbehaves.
takeaways: Reproduce in the passive model before adding control.
Render contact forces, joints, and inertial frames together.
Reset to a known keyframe and change one parameter at a time.
body: First, can the model stand? Turn off all actuators and see whether the pose and contact points look credible. Second, can one joint track a tiny sinusoid? Third, can the full controller work at nominal speed?
Use the viewer overlays aggressively: contact normal and tangent, joint axes, body frames, inertia boxes. Nine out of ten strange dynamics bugs are a joint axis or a collision pair.
Keep a short experiment log next to the model: change, hypothesis, observed, next. Physics debugging fails when changes pile up faster than observations.
